issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma, sexual-violence comments as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless the index event also involved sexual assault or closely related content; nothing else in the profile supports that connection.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal of betrayal by a trusted person is difficult to fit with terrorism as the trauma type unless there was a clear interpersonal betrayal component; the rest of the selected items describe loss of control, helplessness, avoidance, dissociation, and substance use rather than interpersonal betrayal.

vignette:
Rohan, a 37-year-old psychologist, traces the fracture in his life back to a single evening ten months ago. He and his wife were dining on the patio of a crowded restaurant, the city lights diffused by a warm summer haze, when the first sharp cracks echoed from the street. The sound, which he would later identify as gunfire, was followed by screams and the shattering of glass. In the ensuing chaos, he was separated from his wife, thrown to the ground in the stampede, and forced to lie motionless in the near-darkness as the attack unfolded. He remembers the overwhelming feeling of being utterly trapped, a passive object in a world that had suddenly revealed its capacity for random, lethal violence. That sense of profound powerlessness has become the bedrock of his current distress.

In the months that followed, Rohan found that the world had been repainted in shades of threat. The sharp crack of a car backfiring outside his office window would send a jolt of ice through his veins, his heart hammering against his ribs. In the immediate aftermath of such a trigger, he would find himself cancelling his next appointment, reasoning that he was in no state to help anyone. He began keeping a flask of whiskey in his desk drawer, a small, illicit comfort to blunt the edges of the hypervigilance. Waking up in the middle of the night, plunged into the disorienting dark, was even worse. The sudden return to consciousness in the silent house would instantly evoke the memory of lying on the cold pavement, convinced he was about to die. These moments of terror solidified a chilling certainty in his mind: he was fundamentally helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to him or his loved ones.

This conviction that the world is a dangerous place and that he is powerless within it has reshaped his life. He has come to believe that his only recourse is to shrink his world to a manageable size. He began referring his more complex trauma cases to colleagues, telling himself it was for the client's best interest, but knowing it was a way to avoid anything that could be stressful. When the weight of his thoughts becomes too much, especially in the evenings, he retreats into elaborate daydreams, losing hours as he drifts off into a world of his own where nothing can touch him. His wife has commented on his emotional distance, his vacant stares. This retreat, meant to protect him, only serves to deepen his sense of alienation. He catches his reflection and feels a wave of self-loathing; the person he has become is unrecognisable to him, a ghost haunting the life of a man who once felt competent and engaged.

The very strategies Rohan employs to manage his fear now feed the cycle that traps him. His increased reliance on alcohol for sleep has led to a fragmented, unrestful state, causing him to wake up suddenly in the dark several times a week. Each time, he is plunged back into the terror of the attack, his trigger for nighttime reactivated by the very substance he uses to escape it. His professional avoidance has also made him more sensitive; because he so carefully curates his environment to be free of stress, any unexpected demand or sudden change of plans feels like an overwhelming loss of control, another potent trigger. The more he avoids, the more the world seems to demand avoidance, and the more he sees himself as broken.

He has come to therapy because he feels he is on the verge of losing everything that once defined him. Last week, his wife found the flask in his office, her expression a mixture of fear and disappointment that felt more painful than any loud noise. He is a psychologist who cannot manage his own mind, a husband who is emotionally absent, a man who no longer recognises himself. He is terrified that this new, fractured self is permanent, but a small part of him hopes that it is still possible to find his way back to the man he was before the night the world broke open.
